newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Canberra hits New Zealand's 'contrary' diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Canberra hits New Zealand's 'contrary' diplomacy.

text.p: A top secret Australian report has accused neighbouring New Zealand of deliberately spoiling Australian foreign policy in a bid to hide Wellington's growing dependence on Canberra.
The 93-page document -- marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian eyes only -- warns New Zealand sometimes takes a contrary stand just to underline its own fading independence.

The paper was prepared by treasury and foreign department officials for Treasurer Peter Costello as a briefing for the summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in the tropical resort town of Cairns earlier this month.

Publication by Reuters of some details of the briefing -- which also outlined embarrassing personal habits of Costello's 15 guests -- has sparked a political and diplomatic row for Australia's Liberal-National government.

The briefing says New Zealand -- the South Pacific's biggest power after Australia -- increasingly depends on Australia in defence and for trade, through the Closer Economic Relations (CER) free trade agreement.

But it says Wellington sometimes frustrated Canberra's efforts to press economic reform on the region's shaky economies. "Because New Zealand politicians are less able to preserve the fiction of equality with Australia, they are attracted to gestures that underline New Zealand sovereignty and freedom of action," it said.
"New Zealand's growing dependence on Australia, especially in CER and defence -- in which New Zealand capacity is weak and declining -- underlines the strategic inequality of the relationship.
"But wanting to differentiate itself from Australia, New Zealand can act in ways which complicate Australian diplomacy."

Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer ordered his department into damage control after publication of the report's details, instructing heads of mission in the South Pacific to tell their host governments the document does not represent the government's views.
Nauru and the Cook Islands have condemned the briefing as offensive and wrong and Australia's Labor opposition attacked it as patronising and contemptuous.
Australian Workplace Relations Minister Peter Reith, one of the coalition's most senior officials, said on Sunday the document did not represent the government's views.

And he said its comments were not as damaging to Australia's foreign relations as bungles by the former Labor administration, such as former prime minister Paul Keating's description of Malaysian leader Mahathir Mohamad as recalcitrant.
The 1993 recalcitrant row prompted a severe chill in relations and at one stage threatened trade.
The Costello paper, in a scathing indictment of mismanagement, corruption and the personal habits of political leaders, warns of impending economic disaster in several South Pacific countries.

It was left on a table in a public area at the summit where it was obtained by Reuters. Australian officials would not comment on the paper or its contents, but a senior official privately confirmed it was genuine.
Most South Pacific economies are afflicted by low growth, high debt, bloated public sectors, growing populations and weak or virtually non-existent private sectors.

Australia and New Zealand are the forum's biggest economies, dwarfing the poorer island nations -- the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.
